title: Fisher-Rao Sensitivity for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Deep Neural Networks
claim: Familiar inputs sit on a flat region of the prediction manifold, while anomalous inputs sit on a steep one, so sensitivity separates them.
layout: 2 panels, side-by-side split by a vertical line, math captions below
description: Two side-by-side sketch plots are separated by a thick vertical line. Both have a horizontal axis θ and a vertical axis p(y|x, θ̂). The left panel is for an in-distribution input. Its red curve S_x^I is nearly flat, and a short blue double-headed tangent arrow sits at the dotted θ̂ marker. The right panel is for an out-of-distribution input. Its red curve S_x^O is a steep S-shape, and a long blue tangent arrow at θ̂ slopes sharply downward. Dotted lines drop from the curves to the axes at θ̂. Red set-definition equations sit under each panel, for example S_x = {p(y|x,θ) | θ ∈ Θ}. Red is used for the manifolds and blue for the tangents. The eye goes first to the contrast between the flat curve and the steep one.
caption: Fisher–Rao sensitivity distinguishes ID from OoD. For a fixed input x, varying the parameters θ traces the statistical manifold Sx = p(y|x, θ) | θ ∈Θ. At the trained parameters
abstract: Deep neural networks often remain overconfident on Out-of-Distribution (OoD) inputs. We revisit this problem through Riemannian information geometry. We model the network's predictions as a statistical manifold and find that OoD inputs exhibit higher local Fisher-Rao sensitivity. By quantifying this sensitivity with the trace of the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), we derive a unifying geometric connection between two common OoD signals: feature magnitude and output uncertainty. Analyzing the limitations of this multiplicative form, we extend our analysis using a product manifold construction. This provides a theoretical framework for the robust additive scores used in state-of-the-art (SOTA) detectors and motivates our final, competitive method.
